blocks.text: “Thanks, and thanks, and thanks again for your sweet letter. It was so nice to be able to tell you and to have your sympathy.

“My dear, when it rains, it pours—things come all at once. How true the old sayings are. Here I am. I will be twenty in September, and yet I never had a marriage proposal until today—not a real proposal. And today I have had three! Just imagine! THREE proposals in one day! Isn’t it awful! I feel sorry, really and truly sorry, for two of the poor men. Oh, Mina, I am so happy that I don’t know what to do with myself. And three proposals! But, for goodness’ sake, don’t tell any of the girls. Otherwise, they would get all sorts of wild, unrealistic ideas. If they did not get at least six on their very first day at home, they would imagine they were being treated unfairly and without respect. Some girls are so full of foolish pride! Mina dear, you and I are engaged. Soon we are going to settle down seriously and sensibly as old married women. So we can strongly look down on that kind of foolish pride. Well, I must tell you about the three. But you must keep it a secret from everyone, dear, except Jonathan, of course. You will tell him, because I would certainly tell Arthur if I were in your place. A woman should tell her husband everything—don’t you think so, dear? And I must be fair. Men like women, and certainly their wives, to be just as fair as they are. And women, I am afraid, are not always quite as fair as they should be. Well, my dear, number One came just before lunch. I told you about him. He is Dr. John Seward, the man from the mental hospital, with the strong jaw and the good forehead. He was very calm on the outside, but he was nervous even so. Clearly, he had been training himself in all sorts of little things, and he remembered them. Still, he almost managed to sit down on his silk hat. Men do not usually do that when they are calm! Then, when he wanted to look relaxed, he kept playing with a small, sharp medical knife in a way that made me almost scream. He spoke to me very directly and honestly, Mina. He told me how dear I was to him, even though he had known me so little. And he told me what his life would be like with me to help him and keep him cheerful. He was going to tell me how unhappy he would be if I did not care for him. But when he saw me cry, he said that he was a cruel brute and would not add to my trouble at that moment. Then he stopped speaking and asked if I could come to love him over time. When I shook my head, his hands trembled. He hesitated a little, and then he asked me if I already cared for anyone else. He asked this in a very kind, polite way. He said he did not want to force me to share my private feelings. He only wanted to know, because if a woman’s heart was free, a man might have hope. And then, Mina, I felt a kind of duty to tell him that there was someone. I told him only that much. Then he stood up. He looked very strong and very serious as he took both my hands in his. He said he hoped I would be happy. And he told me that if I ever needed a friend, I must think of him as one of my best friends. Oh, Mina dear, I can’t help crying, and you must forgive me because this letter is all stained and smudged. Having someone ask to marry you is all very nice, and all that sort of thing. But it isn’t at all a happy thing when you have to see a poor man go away looking completely broken-hearted. You know that he loves you honestly. And you also know that, no matter what he may say at the moment, you are going completely out of his life. My dear, I must stop here for now. I feel so miserable, even though I am so happy.

“Arthur has just gone, and I feel more cheerful than when I stopped. So I can go on telling you about the day. Well, my dear, number Two came after lunch. He is such a nice man, an American from Texas. He looks so young and so fresh that it seems almost impossible he has been to so many places and had such adventures. I feel sympathy for poor Desdemona when such a dangerous stream was poured into her ear, even by a black man. I suppose we women are such cowards that we think a man will save us from our fears. And so we marry him. I know now what I would do if I were a man and wanted to make a girl love me. No, I don’t—because there was Mr. Morris telling us his stories, and Arthur never told any, and yet— My dear, I am getting a little ahead of myself. Mr. Quincey P. Morris found me alone. It seems that a man always does find a girl alone. No, he doesn’t, because Arthur tried twice to create an opportunity, with me helping him all I could. I am not ashamed to say it now. Before I go on, I must tell you that Mr. Morris doesn’t always use informal slang expressions. That is, he never speaks that way to strangers or in front of them, because he is really well educated and has wonderful, very polite manners. But he found out that it amused me to hear him speak American slang. Whenever I was there, and there was no one around to be shocked, he said such funny things. I am afraid, my dear, that he has to invent it all, because it fits exactly into whatever else he has to say. But slang is like that. I do not know myself if I will ever speak slang. And I do not know if Arthur likes it, because I have never heard him use any yet. Well, Mr. Morris sat down beside me and looked as happy and cheerful as he could. Even so, I could see that he was very nervous. He took my hand in his, and said so very sweetly:
